note: Compact style guide the writer and the script judge load. Numbers come from the corpus study (python -m pipeline.writer analyze); see style_stats.json for the measured values behind them. Examples are invented.

rules: Keep it frightening through what is heard, half seen or wrong: a voice that should not be there, a detail that does not fit, a thing that moved. Never describe blood, wounds, bodies or pain.
The threat speaks. Give the thing, the voice or the stranger at least two short lines, and mark its voice as slightly wrong.
Use a false relief before the turn: one beat where it seems over.
End on the worst moment or one line after it. Do not explain the monster and do not rescue anyone in the last line.
Open with the rule of the world and its cost in one sentence.
Show three quick, literal consequences of the rule before the narrator turns to their own problem.
The last line returns to the first line with one new clause.
First line is the hook: the strangest true thing in the story, said plainly, in 14 words or fewer. No greeting, no scene setting, no 'this is a story about'.
By 30 words a new viewer can say what the story is about.
Narrate in first person, past tense, as the person it happened to. Rules of a world are present tense.

One new filmable fact per sentence: something a camera can see or a microphone can hear. Thoughts, realisations and feelings become actions: not 'I was terrified' but 'I backed into the corner'; not 'Then I understood' but the thing that was seen.
Short sentences. Most are 4 to 10 words; a fragment is a sentence. No sentence over 22 words.
Words a ten-year-old says. Concrete nouns, plain verbs, contractions.
Wherever a character says, texts, writes or whispers something, make it a line of its own with that character as the speaker. The narrator never quotes.
Dialogue is spoken, short and incomplete the way speech is: 2 to 12 words, contractions, a name or a pet name, no explaining. The first spoken line arrives in the first third.
Lead into a spoken line with a short narrator beat that ends on a comma or a colon ('Then I heard my mother's voice.'), or let it stand alone. Never follow it with 'she said'.
The narrator never introduces themselves ('I'm Sam, the night clerk'). If the narrator needs a name, another character says it.
Escalate in steps: normal, one wrong detail, a worse one, a moment of relief, the turn. The turn falls between 60% and 90% of the way through.
The last line is 12 words or fewer and lands the turn: a twist, a cliffhanger, or a return to the first line. No moral, no summary, no 'subscribe'.
Cut every word that does not move the picture: no 'suddenly', 'very', 'really', 'literally', 'little did I know', 'I couldn't believe my eyes'.
Keep the source's premise, its best image and its ending. Merge or drop side characters, travel, backstory and explanation.
Family-safe: no gore, no slurs, no sexual content, no self-harm, no real brands or real people.
